The shipped fix landed 2026-05-03 in commit \`36b2bba\` with detect-and-skip in commit \`06aa938\` 2026-05-04, but NEXT_SESSION.md was authored end-of-session 2026-05-05 without checking git log or the live \`bellows.py\`. When NEXT_SESSION.md, a BACKLOG entry, or a CEO statement asserts "the fix is still pending," the Planner's first move is to grep for the recommended code, not to design the diagnostic. The cost is one tool call; the savings are an entire diagnostic→executable session that would have re-derived shipped work. **Lesson 2 — population audits are a cheap, high-leverage diagnostic technique.** When a recurring failure has accumulated multiple reproductions and a "fix needed" hypothesis, a population audit (enumerate all reproductions in a date window, classify each by pre-fix / accepted-exposure / post-fix-gap) is often the right first diagnostic — it produces a count and a verdict, not a recommendation, and it answers "is this still a bug or is it a known-and-accepted constraint?" Cost: ~10 minutes of agent time, ~$0.20. The 2026-05-05 BACKLOG #1 audit consumed 9 minutes and produced a clean close. On `queue.Empty` returns None. **`stop(self)`:** no-op for now — daemon thread dies with the process. **Implement `tests/test_notifier_server.py`** with three tests: (1) `test_push_success` — mocks `requests.post` to return a mock with `status_code=200`, calls `notifier.push("app", "user", "title", "msg")`, asserts returns True; (2) `test_push_failure` — mocks `requests.post` to return `status_code=400`, asserts returns False; (3) `test_server_respond` — creates `ResponseServer(port=15432)`, calls `start()`, sends a POST to `http://localhost:15432/respond` with JSON `{"decision": "continue"}` via `requests.post`, calls `wait_for_response(timeout=3)`, asserts returned dict has `decision == "continue"`. **Run tests:** `python -m pytest tests/test_notifier_server.py -v` — all must pass. Execute Step {current_step + 1}."` ; (9) call `runner.run_step(next_prompt, project_path, config["default_model"], session_id=parsed["session_id"])`; (10) update parsed, increment step, record to db; (11) on loop exit (final step complete): call `notifier.notify_complete(...)` with total cost summed across all steps. The shipped fix (file-checksum snapshot) was reverted via plan \`executable-revert-snapshot-fix-and-reopen-backlog-2026-05-01\`. **Lesson:** when an SA recommends a fix shape, the Planner's Rule 22 verification of the diagnostic must include the question: "If I trace through the original observed bug step-by-step, does this fix actually prevent it?" Rule 22's check (b) ("does the file's content actually answer the original questions") interrogates substance, not just structural completeness — load-bearing claims in agent recommendations need to be traced, not accepted. |` **Entry 2 — test naming vs assertion mismatch:** insert this as a new row immediately after Entry 1: `| 2026-05-01 | Test names that imply a property must have assertions that verify that property. The mismatch was visible in the test's own commentary ("plan_b_file.txt DOES appear (it genuinely changed on disk) — but that's correct behavior for snapshot-based diff"). The Planner specified the test in the plan; the agent implemented it faithfully; QA passed it. The name-vs-assertion gap created false assurance. **Lesson:** when the Planner specifies a test in a plan, the assertion must encode the property the test name implies. If the property cannot be encoded as an assertion (because the implementation doesn't actually have the property), the test name is misleading and either the property or the name needs to change. Planner polling of Bellows verdict requests\n\nWhen the Planner dispatches a plan to Bellows (Layer 1 execution engine), Bellows posts verdict request files to `bellows/verdicts/pending/` whenever a plan pauses — between steps, at gate failures, at QA checkpoints, or at final-step close. The Planner has no automatic notification when these files appear. Without discipline, the Planner only discovers a verdict when the CEO relays a Pushover notification or asks the Planner to check. This breaks Rule 22's verification loop: Rule 22 assumes the Planner reads deposited files after an agent reports Complete, but in the Bellows flow the "agent reports Complete" signal IS a verdict request file the Planner does not see.\n\nRule 25 closes this loop. Every turn in a conversation where the Planner has at least one plan outstanding in Bellows, the Planner scans `bellows/verdicts/pending/` for verdict request files whose filename contains the slug of a session-dispatched plan. If a matching verdict file is found, the Planner reads it, routes on the `Pause Reason Code` field, and either performs Rule 22 verification on the `Deposit` field or stops and reports to the CEO.\n\n**What counts as a session-dispatched plan:** Any plan the Planner has deposited to `knowledge/decisions/` during the current conversation, AND any plan the Planner has re-authorized during the current conversation (e.g., via manual bootstrap after a Bellows bypass). The Planner tracks these plans internally — by slug — as part of normal conversation state. Verdicts from plans dispatched in prior sessions or by other Planner instances are NOT this Planner's responsibility and should be ignored by Rule 25's scan (the CEO handles those via the normal Bellows notification path).\n\n**Scan mechanics:** Once per conversation turn where an active session-plan exists, the Planner calls `Filesystem:list_directory` on the `bellows/verdicts/pending/` directory (read-only; the Planner has no write access there and does not need any). It filters the listing for filenames matching the pattern `verdict-request-<session-plan-slug>-step-*.md` where `<session-plan-slug>` is any plan the Planner has dispatched this session. For any match, the Planner calls `Filesystem:read_text_file` on the verdict file and extracts four fields: `Plan:`, `Step:`, `Pause Reason Code:`, and `Deposit:`. If the file is missing any of those fields, that is itself a Rule 22 verification failure — the Planner stops and reports the schema violation to the CEO.\n\n**Pause reason routing:** The `Pause Reason Code` field determines whether the Planner auto-proceeds to Rule 22 verification or stops and reports. The routing is deliberately conservative — only two codes authorize auto-proceed, everything else stops:\n\n| Pause Reason Code | Routing |\n|---|---|\n| `auto_close_disabled` | Auto-proceed to Rule 22 verification on the Deposit field. This is the normal between-step pause for plans with auto_close disabled. |\n| `qa_checkpoint` | Auto-proceed to Rule 22 verification on the Deposit field. This is the standard DEV→QA handoff signal. |\n| `gate_failure` | Stop and report to CEO. A Bellows gate tripped — the Planner does NOT mechanically approve plans that tripped gates, regardless of whether the Deposit file passes Rule 22. Quote the gate failure text from the verdict file's `## Gate Failures` section in the report. |\n| `scope_violation` | Stop and report to CEO. The agent modified files outside the plan's declared scope. Same no-mechanical-approval rule as gate_failure. |\n| Any other code (including unknown, missing, or future codes) | Stop and report to CEO. Conservative fallback — the Planner does not guess at the safety of unfamiliar pause reasons. |\n\n**Rule 22 routing on auto-proceed codes:** When the Pause Reason Code authorizes auto-proceed, the Planner takes the path in the verdict file's `Deposit:` field and applies Rule 22's (a)–(e) checks to that path. If the Deposit field is `none` (no deposit declared for that step), the Planner reports the verdict to the CEO for judgment — "none" is not a failure but it is not a Rule 22 pass either, and the CEO decides whether the step should have declared a deposit. If Rule 22 passes, the Planner reports the pass to the CEO ("Step N QA verification passed, safe to close Bellows verdict") and the CEO resolves the verdict via the normal Bellows workflow. If Rule 22 fails at any of (a)–(e), the Planner reports the failure in full per Rule 22's existing escalation language.\n\n**Gate-failure guard (load-bearing):** Rule 25 is designed to MECHANIZE routine verification, not to automate approval. The pause-reason taxonomy is the safety layer. If Bellows reports a gate failure or scope violation, that is a signal the plan did something unexpected — the Planner treats it as a halt-and-report condition no matter how clean the Deposit file looks. The CEO is the authority on whether a gate failure is a false positive (e.g., BACKLOG #6's deposit-path parser false positives observed on Plan B's QA step) or a genuine problem. The Planner does NOT decide this unilaterally.\n\n**Relationship to Rule 22:** Rule 25 is a TRIGGER and ROUTER for Rule 22, not a replacement. Rule 22 still defines the verification checks (a)–(e) that the Planner applies to any deposited file. Rule 25 adds the Bellows-dispatched discovery path: when the deposit reference comes from a verdict request file (not an inline CEO "done" signal), Rule 25 is how the Planner finds the deposit; Rule 22 is how the Planner verifies it.\n\n**Physical cleanup is CEO responsibility:** The Planner does not rename, delete, or otherwise modify files in `bellows/verdicts/pending/`. Read-only access. Physical cleanup of stranded verdict files is a CEO `rm` action (see BACKLOG #1 scope_check race for the broader cleanup-automation discussion).\n\n**Operational note — this rule is not blocked by BACKLOG #4 or #5:** The Bellows-side reliability items (filesystem watcher reliability, step state across re-claim) operate on the Bellows dispatch side. Rule 25 operates on the Planner's read side — it scans files Bellows has already written. The two are structurally independent. Rule 25 can be adopted immediately and will continue to work correctly as BACKLOG #4 and #5 are resolved.\n\n### Diagnostic Prompt Engineering`. Rule 25 operates on the Planner's read side — it scans files Bellows has already written. The two are structurally independent. Rule 25 can be adopted immediately and will continue to work correctly as BACKLOG #4 and #5 are resolved.\n\n### 26. Deposits field convention\n\nEvery step in every executable and diagnostic plan MUST declare its deposits via a `**Deposits:**` field. The field lists every file the step will create or write to — deposit files, dev logs, QA reports, evidence files, specialist syncs, any file the step is responsible for producing. The list is the canonical enumeration; anything not on it is not a deposit of that step.\n\n**Why this rule exists:** Prior plans referenced deposits inside the prose of each step ("deposit findings to `path/to/file.md`", "write the QA report to `path/to/report.md`"), which forced Bellows's `deposit_exists` gate to keyword-scan the entire step text for path-like strings. That scan has tripped repeatedly on non-deposit paths — specialist-file content embedded inside plans, test-fixture strings embedded inside QA smoke tests, documentation examples referencing paths they don't create. Every false positive stranded a plan in `verdict-pending-*` state and required manual CEO bootstrap to resume. BACKLOG #6 enumerates the failure class. Rule 26 establishes a declarative field so future plans have a single unambiguous source of truth for deposits; a subsequent Bellows-side plan will extend the deposit parser to read the declared field and ignore prose-embedded paths.\n\n**Field format and placement:** The field lives inside the step prompt, near the end, separated from surrounding prose by the bold marker `**Deposits:**` followed by a bulleted list. The format is:\n\n```\n**Deposits:**\n- `path/to/first/deposit.md`\n- `path/to/second/deposit.md`\n```\n\nEach bullet holds exactly one path wrapped in backticks. Paths are project-relative (e.g., `bellows/knowledge/qa/my-report.md`) unless the deposit target is an absolute governance-root path (e.g., `/Users/marklehn/Desktop/GitHub/PLANNER_TEMPLATE.md`) — the absolute-path case is rare and reserved for governance edits. The list is complete: every file the step writes to MUST appear. Evidence files (Rule 18) do NOT need individual bullets — list the evidence directory as a single bullet (e.g., `- `bellows/knowledge/qa/evidence/<plan-slug>/` (multiple files per Rule 20 self-check)`), because the Rule 20 self-check already enumerates the individual evidence filenames.\n\n**The "no deposits" case:** If a step makes no deposits at all — pure diagnostic investigation reported in conversation, pure housekeeping with no file writes, etc. — the field is still present, with a single bullet `- none`. Omission of the field is NOT permitted. Explicit `- none` declaration distinguishes "this step intentionally produces no files" from "the author forgot to list the deposits." Bellows's future deposit parser will treat a missing `**Deposits:**` field as a plan authoring error, not a no-deposit step.\n\n**Relationship to Bellows's current deposit parser:** The `extract_primary_deposit()` function currently reads `**Deposit:**` (singular, bold-noun-colon form, cluster A of the 2026-04-18 deposit-path format survey) and does NOT recognize the plural-list form Rule 26 specifies. This is a known parser gap that will be closed by a future gates.py plan. During the gap window, verdict request files written by Bellows for Rule 26-compliant plans will show `Deposit: none` (because the singular-form parser finds nothing to match) even when the plan declares three deposits. This is the expected state during the transition.\n\n**Planner behavior during the parser-gap window:** When Rule 25 surfaces a verdict with `Deposit: none` for a session-plan the Planner knows was written under Rule 26, the Planner does NOT escalate to the CEO as the generic "none" case does. Instead, the Planner reads the plan file directly (via `Filesystem:read_text_file`), extracts the `**Deposits:**` block for the relevant step, and applies Rule 22's (a)–(e) checks to each path in that block. The plan's declared `**Deposits:**` block is canonical; the verdict request's `Deposit` field is advisory during this window. This Planner-side resolution absorbs the parser gap without triggering CEO noise for every Rule 26 plan. Once the gates.py plan ships, the verdict request's `Deposit` field will reflect the declared `**Deposits:**` content directly and this resolution path falls away.\n\n**Retroactive application:** This rule applies to NEW plans written after v4.25 lands. Existing plans (in-progress or in Done/) do NOT require retroactive amendment — legacy plans continue to work under the existing keyword-scan gate (with its known false-positive rate). The Planner does not go back and edit old plans to add the field.\n\n**Interaction with Rule 21 (test scope) and Rule 18 (evidence files):** Rule 26 complements these rules, doesn't replace them. A QA step still declares its test scope in the plan header (Rule 21) and still pipes command output to evidence files (Rule 18). The `**Deposits:**` field lists the QA report file and the evidence directory; it does NOT list each individual evidence filename (Rule 20's self-check already does that). The three rules compose: Rule 21 decides what to test, Rule 18 requires output be captured in evidence files, Rule 20 mechanically verifies those files exist, and Rule 26 declares the overall deposits shape.\n\n**Migration scope:** The governance edit is Rule 26's only scope. A separate future plan will (a) extend the deposit parser in `verdict.py` (or `bellows.py`, wherever `extract_primary_deposit` lives — confirmed today to live in `verdict.py` per Plan B's circular-import avoidance) to recognize the `**Deposits:**` block as a list, (b) change the `deposit_exists` gate in `gates.py` to scope its scan to the declared block only when the plan has one, (c) preserve the legacy keyword-scan fallback for plans without a declared block. That plan is out of scope for Rule 26. Rule 26 ships the governance convention alone so authorship compliance can be observed before Bellows-side enforcement is added.\n\n### Diagnostic Prompt Engineering`. State your choice and the reasoning. Address: query complexity, write complexity, backward compatibility with existing reads, migration cost, performance implications for gate 8 lookups (which run per-invoice). **(2) State transition matrix.** Enumerate every state a `contract_fuel_table` (and `carrier_fuel_table`) row can be in, with explicit pre/post conditions for each transition. Required boundary states: last bracket of a contract (no successor floor — what does the "implicit ceiling" become? Infinity? Contract-declared max? NULL?); single-bracket contract (n=1); two-bracket contract (n=2); contract with a pre-existing stored gap (e.g. brackets at 3.00–3.04 and 3.10–3.14 where the carrier genuinely doesn't price 3.05–3.09); brackets with `price_ceiling IS NULL` in legacy data; brackets where `price_ceiling < price_floor` (data corruption — does the migration normalize or flag?); brackets where `price_ceiling != next_row.price_floor - .001` (the precision-gap case we're fixing — silently absorb or flag?). (2) A line containing `origin_type` signals the start of a lanes section. (3) If NEITHER header is found but the data contains both area-like rows (short, ~4-5 fields) and lane-like rows (longer, ~9 fields), prepend the appropriate headers to each portion. To detect: split raw lines, check if any line starts with or contains `area_code` — that's the areas header. Check if any line contains `origin_type` — that's the lanes header. Split at the boundary between the two sections. Each section includes its header row. If a section is missing its header, prepend it using the known column order from the Copilot prompt. **Also remove the 400 error for combined data** that was added in the previous fix (executable-lanes-reparse-header-order). The combined format should now be handled, not rejected. **Also ensure** that when the split succeeds, the areas portion goes to `_import_areas_section` and the lanes portion goes through the lanes parser, with combined counts returned. No routes wired yet — this is foundation only.** **(1) Create `engines/rate_paste_parser.py`.** Module exports a single public function `parse_rate_grid(raw_text: str) -> dict` that returns `{"tariff_name": str|None, "effective_date": str|None, "origin_zip": str|None, "dest_zip": str|None, "rates": list[dict], "errors": list[str], "warnings": list[str]}`. Each rate dict has keys: `freight_class, weight_break, rate_per_cwt, weight_min, weight_max`. Also export module-level constants: `FREIGHT_CLASSES` (list of 18 canonical NMFC classes: "50", "55", "60", "65", "70", "77.5", "85", "92.5", "100", "110", "125", "150", "175", "200", "250", "300", "400", "500"), `WEIGHT_BREAKS` (list of tuples: `("0", 0, 499), ("500", 500, 999), ("1000", 1000, 1999), ("2000", 2000, 4999), ("5000", 5000, 9999), ("10000", 10000, 19999), ("20000", 20000, 29999), ("30000", 30000, 39999), ("40000", 40000, 44999)`), `WB_ALIASES` (dict mapping Navisphere codes to canonical codes — copy from existing `web/rates.py:78-94`), `WEIGHT_BREAK_BOUNDS` (dict built from WEIGHT_BREAKS). These constants live in the parser module and can be re-exported by `web/rates.py` later during Phase 4 cleanup. **(2) Metadata parsing.** The parser first consumes metadata lines before the grid. Metadata keys recognized: `TARIFF`, `EFFECTIVE`, `ORIGIN`, `DEST`. A metadata line has format `KEY: value`. Metadata ends at the first blank line OR the first line that is not a metadata line. Store parsed metadata in the result dict: `tariff_name` from `TARIFF:`, `effective_date` from `EFFECTIVE:`, `origin_zip` from `ORIGIN:` (use `web.utils.normalize_zip` if possible, otherwise just `.strip()`), `dest_zip` from `DEST:`. **(3) Tariff name rejection rule.** If `tariff_name` is None, empty, or equals "UNKNOWN" (case-insensitive) after metadata parsing, return immediately with `errors = ["No tariff name found in paste. Rates cannot be verified without a tariff name. Re-screenshot including the document header."]` and `rates = []`. Do NOT attempt to parse the grid. This is the primary rejection rule from the roadmap. **(4) Grid header parsing — structural rule, NOT positional.** After metadata, the remaining lines are the grid. Split the first non-blank line by tab. If the tab split produces only 1 element (no tabs), fall back to comma split. Call this `header_parts`. Build `wb_columns` as a **list of canonical wb_codes only** (NOT tuples with indices): iterate `header_parts`, for each cell call `cell.strip().upper().replace(" ", "")`, if it matches `WB_ALIASES`, append the canonical code to `wb_columns`. **Skip any leading empty cell** but do NOT use the cell's index position. The result is a flat list like `["0", "500", "1000", "2000", "5000", "10000", "20000", "30000", "40000"]` in the order they appeared in the header. This list's length defines how many rate columns each data row must have. If `wb_columns` is empty after scanning, return with `errors = ["Could not detect weight break columns in header row. Expected codes like L5C, M5C, M1M, M2M, etc."]`. **(5) Data row parsing — enforce class-at-0, rates-at-1..N.** For each data row after the header: split by tab or comma (use the same delimiter as the header). Strip each cell. **`parts[0]` is ALWAYS the freight class**, regardless of what the header looked like. **Rates are ALWAYS at `parts[1:1+len(wb_columns)]`**, one rate per entry in `wb_columns` in order. If the row has fewer than `1 + len(wb_columns)` cells, pad with empty strings (missing trailing rates are allowed). Reject rows where `parts[0]` is not in `FREIGHT_CLASSES` (with normalization: `"077.5"` → `"77.5"`, `"050"` → `"50"`, etc). Skip known header/footer words: `class, nmfc, total, minimum, min, note, notes`. For minimum charge lines (`Minimum charge weight > 0 : $85.00`), extract the value and store in the result dict as `min_charge` (optional key). **(6) Per-row sanity guards.** For each successfully parsed row, apply three guards before emitting the rate records: (a) **Rate equals class guard** — for every rate value in the row, if `float(rate) == float(freight_class)` (within 0.001 tolerance), append warning `"Row with class {class}: rate {rate} equals class value — likely column misalignment, row rejected"` and SKIP the entire row. (b) **Rate range guard** — if `rate < 0.01 or rate > 1000.00`, append warning `"Row with class {class}, weight break {wb}: rate {rate} out of plausible range [0.01, 1000.00], cell skipped"` and skip just that cell (not the whole row). (c) **Non-numeric guard** — if the rate cell cannot be parsed as float after stripping `$` and `,`, append warning `"Row with class {class}, weight break {wb}: invalid rate {value}"` and skip just that cell. Valid rates produce a dict `{freight_class, weight_break, rate_per_cwt, weight_min, weight_max}` appended to `rates`. `weight_min` and `weight_max` come from `WEIGHT_BREAK_BOUNDS[wb_code]`. **(7) Canonical name matching helper.** Also export `match_canonical_doc(db, tariff_name: str, effective_date: str|None = None) -> int|None`. Implementation: query `SELECT id, doc_name FROM global_documents WHERE doc_type = 'base_rate_tariff'`. For each row, normalize both sides by lowercasing and stripping whitespace. If `effective_date` is provided, the expected match format is `"{tariff_name} ({effective_date})"` — check both "exact match on full canonical" and "tariff_name prefix match" (in case some docs haven't been renamed yet per Phase 1's open question). Return the matching `id` or `None`. Do NOT create new docs from this function — auto-create is Phase 3 concern. This helper is tested but not yet wired to routes. **(8) Module structure.** File header comment explaining: purpose (new rate paste parser replacing the broken positional parser in web/rates.py), reference to diagnostic file `knowledge/research/rate-grid-leading-tab-2026-04-08.md`, and the structural rule (class at parts[0], rates at parts[1:]). Type hints on all public functions. No Flask imports — this module is framework-agnostic and testable in isolation. Database access only through the `db` parameter passed to `match_canonical_doc`. **(9) Tests.** Create `tests/test_rate_paste_parser.py` with at minimum these test cases: (a) `test_input_a_leading_tab_preserved` — the canonical Navisphere format from diagnostic Input A, asserts class 50 L5C rate = 45.20, class 50 M5C rate = 38.10, etc. (b) `test_input_b_leading_tab_stripped` — diagnostic Input B (the bug case), asserts that after parsing, class 50 L5C rate = 45.20 (NOT 50), class 50 M5C rate = 38.10. This is the regression test that locks in the fix. (c) `test_input_c_comma_separated` — diagnostic Input C, same assertions. (d) `test_missing_tariff_name_rejected` — grid with no `TARIFF:` line, expects error "No tariff name found..." and empty rates list. (e) `test_unknown_tariff_name_rejected` — `TARIFF: UNKNOWN`, same rejection. (f) `test_rate_equals_class_rejected` — a crafted row where one rate happens to equal the class value, expects warning and row skipped. (g) `test_rate_out_of_range` — a rate of 2000.00 (too high) and 0.001 (too low), expects warnings and those cells skipped but valid rates retained. (h) `test_metadata_parsed` — full metadata block (TARIFF, EFFECTIVE, ORIGIN, DEST) followed by grid, asserts all metadata fields populated. (i) `test_minimum_charge_extracted` — grid with `Minimum charge weight > 0 : $85.00` line, asserts `min_charge == 85.00`. (j) `test_freight_class_normalization` — rows with `"077.5"`, `"050"`, `"92.5"` all parse to canonical `"77.5"`, `"50"`, `"92.5"`. (k) `test_header_footer_words_skipped` — rows starting with `"Class"`, `"Total"`, `"Notes"` are silently skipped without errors. (l) `test_empty_wb_columns_error` — header with no recognized weight break codes, expects error. (m) `test_match_canonical_doc_exact` — seed a global_documents row, call `match_canonical_doc`, assert it returns the id. (n) `test_match_canonical_doc_no_match` — call with a name that doesn't exist, assert returns None. Rule 8's existing language ("every plan must include a QA step — no exceptions, not even for Small tier or single-file fixes") already covers this; no rule-text edit needed. The QA step for markdown-only plans is intentionally lightweight: (a) verify each edited file exists on disk and contains the new content via grep for key phrases from the edits, (b) verify the commit hash exists in the correct repo's git log and matches the plan's stated commit message, (c) run the Rule 20 self-check with whatever evidence files the plan declares (often just a grep_deliverables.txt and git_log.txt). No pytest, no PRAGMA, no live smoke test — but also no skipping the separate-agent verification gate. The rationale is Rule 8's original one: QA is not a test-running role, it is a separation-of-concerns role. A DEV/Documentation agent that just wrote an edit has a built-in incentive to mark it done; a QA agent reading the edit fresh has a built-in incentive to find what's missing. That incentive split is the load-bearing property, not the presence of tests. Removing the QA step for markdown plans would save ~3 minutes per plan and lose the verification gate that catches agents self-reporting Complete on edits that didn't fully land. **Meta-lesson:** when a rule has an exception pattern emerging in practice, the correct response is usually to reinforce the rule explicitly (Position A), not to formalize the exception (Position B). Exceptions formalized tend to expand; rules reinforced tend to hold. |\n| 2026-04-20 | v4.26 governance sweep: six edits derived from a diagnostic pass over BACKLOG items deferred since v4.18 — (1) Rule 20 `[x]` dead code removal from POSITIVE_STATUS_TOKENS list; (2) Plan File Structure: commit-repo-location rule for governance-root edits; (3) Rule 14 state-transition enumeration extension; (4) Rule 13 fourth anchoring technique for contract-section UI; (5) Lessons entry codifying Position A (no markdown-only QA carve-out, immediately above); (6) this summary row.
